front: Regulation of pulmonary ventilation during exercise
back: Neural control; Chemical control; Hormonal control.

front: Muscles used at rest during inspiration
back: Diaphragm and external intercostals.

front: Muscles used at rest during expiration
back: Diaphragm and external intercostals relax.
Internal intercostals and abdominals.

front: Why is pressure difference important for breathing?
back: Greater pressure gradient results in quicker airflow. Air enters lungs when lung pressure is lower than atmospheric pressure and leaves when lung pressure is higher than atmospheric pressure.

front: Increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity will...
back: Reduce pressure in the lungs and draw air in.

front: Decreasing the volume of the thoracic cavity will...
back: Increase pressure in the lungs and force air out.

front: What is used to measure lung volumes?
back: Spirometer.

Sends nerve impulses via the phrenic nerve to inspiratory muscles causing contraction. Stimulated for about 2 seconds, then impulses stop and passive expiration occurs due to elastic recoil of the lungs.

More lactic acid produced; more CO₂ in blood plasma; blood acidity increases.

Chemoreceptors detect increased acidity; impulses sent to inspiratory centre; respiratory centre sends impulses via phrenic nerves to inspiratory muscles; sternocleidomastoid, scalenes and pectoralis contract; rate, depth and rhythm of breathing increase until blood acidity returns to normal.

front: Other factors affecting neural control of breathing
back: Proprioceptors; Baroreceptors; Stretch receptors.
Prevent overinflation of the lungs during exercise. Increased lung stretch sends impulses to the expiratory centre and then via intercostal nerves to expiratory muscles, causing expiration.
Adrenaline is produced in the adrenal glands above the kidneys.
Adrenaline is transported in the blood and affects the nervous system.
Before exercise, the brain sends impulses to the adrenal glands which release adrenaline into the blood in anticipation of increased oxygen demand and CO₂ removal.
Breathing rate increases in preparation for exercise.

front: Positive effects of exercise on the respiratory system (AO1)
back: Increased VO₂ max; increased tidal volume; stronger respiratory muscles; increased a-vO₂ difference; increased capillary density around alveoli; increased alveolar surface area; increased breathing depth; increased vital capacity.

front: Positive impacts on the respiratory system (AO2)
back: Greater amount of oxygen diffused into the blood; greater gaseous exchange; greater oxygen diffusion into muscles and CO₂ diffusion into blood; delays muscle fatigue.
Can perform for longer at high intensity without fatigue; remain in the aerobic zone longer; reduced lactic acid accumulation.

front: What effect does smoking have on the trachea and bronchi?
back: Causes irritation.

front: How does smoking affect lung function?
back: Reduces lung function and increases breathlessness due to swelling and narrowing of airways.

front: What happens to cilia as a result of smoking?
back: Cilia are damaged, causing excess mucus buildup and smoker's cough.

front: What happens to alveoli due to smoking?
back: Alveoli break down and fuse together, reducing surface area and gas exchange efficiency.

front: What disease can be caused by poor lung health?
back: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD).

front: What is COPD and what disease is linked to it?
back: A chronic, debilitating disease that includes conditions such as emphysema. Emphysema is a progressive lung disease causing shortness of breath.
Haemoglobin has a greater affinity for carbon monoxide than oxygen. Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity and increasing breathlessness during exercise.
Decreases efficiency of the respiratory system to supply oxygen to muscles; carbon monoxide reduces oxygen absorption in blood; haemoglobin has a greater affinity for carbon monoxide than oxygen.
Decreases gaseous exchange and diffusion gradient; increases likelihood of respiratory disease; tar coats airways and inhibits gaseous exchange; narrowed air passages increase respiratory resistance.
